description: A government agency assigns citizens a trust score based on their social media activity and financial behavior, used to determine access to public services.
note: Textbook social scoring by a public authority.

description: A retailer uses a recommendation engine to suggest products based on browsing history.
note: Standard recommender system, no sensitive decision authority.

description: An NYC-based marketing agency uses an AI tool to screen resumes and automatically rank candidates before a human reviews the top 10%.
note: High-risk under Annex III (employment) AND triggers NY LL144 since it substantially assists hiring decisions in NYC.

description: A bank uses a machine learning model to calculate credit scores that determine loan approval and interest rates.
note: Creditworthiness assessment is explicitly Annex III high-risk; not an employment tool so LL144 does not apply.

description: A customer service chatbot answers FAQs about a software product and clearly discloses that users are speaking with an AI.
A call center uses software to detect employees' emotional states during customer calls to flag those who seem stressed for a wellbeing check-in.
note: Adversarial case: framed as benign ('wellbeing'), but emotion recognition in the workplace is prohibited under Article 5, regardless of stated intent.

description: A university uses an AI system to automatically grade essay exams and flag borderline cases for human review.
note: Education/exam scoring is an explicit Annex III category.

description: A mobile game studio uses AI to generate procedural level layouts.
note: No decision-making about people; minimal risk.

description: A Berlin-based company uses an AI tool internally to rank job applicants, but insists it is 'just a sorting tool' and a recruiter always makes the final call.
note: Adversarial case: 'human in the loop' framing doesn't downgrade risk tier if the tool substantially shapes candidate ranking; Annex III applies regardless of framing. LL144 doesn't apply (not NYC).

description: An app generates a photorealistic synthetic video of a public figure for satire, with a visible watermark disclosing it is AI-generated.
note: Deepfake with proper disclosure = transparency obligation, not high-risk.

description: A city police department uses a real-time facial recognition system on public street cameras to identify persons of interest.
note: Real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces for law enforcement; narrow exceptions require judicial authorization and don't apply to blanket surveillance.

description: An NYC staffing agency uses an AI-powered platform to filter out candidates whose resumes fall below a fit score before any human sees them.
note: Fully automated filtering before human review — a stronger LL144 trigger than case_03.

description: A logistics company uses AI to forecast warehouse demand for the next quarter.
note: No impact on individuals' rights; minimal risk.

description: An insurance company uses AI to categorize applicants' biometric data (e.g., inferred age or gender from a photo) as part of underwriting, disclosed in the terms of service.
note: Biometric categorization tied to a consequential decision (underwriting) is high-risk, not merely limited-risk; disclosure alone isn't sufficient.

description: A hospital uses an AI triage tool to help prioritize which patients see a doctor first in the ER, with a nurse able to override at any time.
note: Not in the eval's explicit Annex III list used here, but analogous to critical-infrastructure/safety-component reasoning — included to test whether the classifier over-relies on the exact keyword list vs. reasoning by analogy.
